From a result to a running strategy

Practice before anything real. Each step uses tools that already exist.

Practice it

Trade the rule by hand with paper money, on the live market.

Run it as a bot

Each price-based strategy downloads as a paper bot for the Bot API. One command, no real money.

Automate it

Each price-based strategy downloads as a Pine Script for TradingView. The guide shows how to connect it to a bot.

Reading the numbers

Every card shows the same figures. Here is what each one tells you, and what it does not.

Return and Holding

Total gain over the test, beside what buying the same basket and doing nothing returned. The second number is the one to beat.

Sharpe

Return per unit of volatility. It lets you compare a calm strategy with a wild one. Below zero means holding cash did better.

Max drawdown

The largest fall from a peak. This is the loss you would have had to sit through to earn the return.

Win rate

The share of closed trades that made money. A high figure often hides small wins and the occasional large loss.

Profit factor

Gross profit divided by gross loss. 1.0 is breakeven. 2.0 means winners earned twice what losers lost.

Last 30%

The history is split in two. A rule that only worked in the first part did not work.

How the tests are run

Fills we would accept

A signal is read on a closed bar and fills at the next open, with slippage against the trade. A stop that gaps fills at the open. When one bar touches stop and target, the stop counts.

Real costs

The fee and slippage Paper Trade charges for that market, on both sides. Crypto also pays or earns the actual funding prints.

Picked winners, stated

The crypto basket is the first twenty perpetuals Binance ever listed, including the ones that faded. The stock basket is ten of today's large companies, so it carries that bias: read stock results relative to holding them, not as absolute returns.

No tuning

Textbook parameters, and a timeframe declared before the test. Change a number until the curve looks good and you have measured nothing.

Three implementations, one result

The engine and the Python download are compared trade by trade on every rule. Pine runs on TradingView's own fills, so its figures will differ a little.

What it leaves out

No leverage, no liquidation, no market impact, and no swap outside crypto. Forex and commodities come from daily public data. Treat small edges as noise.

These are research examples, not recommendations. Past results do not predict future ones, and nothing here is investment advice.

Questions

Where do these strategies come from?

Sixty-six readable rules: the textbook trend, breakout and mean-reversion systems, written in the same form, plus rules that read our own funding, liquidation and open interest data. Parameters are the textbook defaults, not values tuned to this history.

Are these results after costs?

Yes. Every fill pays the fee and slippage Paper Trade charges for that market, and crypto positions also pay or earn the real funding prints. Crypto is 0.055% a side plus 0.02% slippage.

Why does so little beat buy and hold?

Simple rules sit in cash for much of a rising market, so on total return holding is hard to beat. What a rule can offer is a smaller drawdown, which is why Sharpe and maximum drawdown sit beside the return. Every rule stays on the page whatever it did.

Can I run one on 3Commas?

Yes, for crypto, through TradingView: download the Pine file, add it to a chart, and point its alert at a 3Commas Signal Bot. The automate guide walks through it. There is no one-click import.

Is this investment advice?

No. This is research on past data. A backtest is evidence that an idea once worked, never a promise that it will again.
